rv.q: What holds the attention is the way Kessler incrementally shifts the power dynamics within the trio, and the lurid weirdness of it all.
Kessler’s play is certainly a springboard for actors, but for audiences, it sags and slumps.
Too often, Forbes Masson’s Harold veers from magical realism into caricature, an avuncular take on a mafia boss.
Unfortunately however, in Treat’s case, the clothes do not make the man and his character struggles to rise above his historical personality failings.
It is still a captivating play and a great reminder of the brilliant world that lurks behind a relatively hidden door on Jermyn Street.
It’s darkly funny and emotionally bruising and well worth catching.
Despite some good performances and American accents from the three actors, by the end we could not care less whether they live or die.

cn.t: Strong performances elevate this 1983 drama about power dynamics between two brothers and a captive, though the production feels uneven and the play's darker currents don't fully land in this small-scale revival.
